paragraphs.text: The transcript of questioning, including exhibits, made under this Division, an affidavit of records, affidavits and answers to written questions, and correcting affidavits under this Division (a) must not be filed and must not be put before the Court except during an application, proceeding or at trial, and (b) may be filed and put before the Court only as permitted by these rules, in which case the person relying on the documents filed must provide the material in writing or in any other form permitted by the Court.

paragraphs.text: (1) The information and records described in subrule (2) must be treated as confidential and may only be used by the recipient of the information or record for the purpose of carrying on the action in which the information or record was provided or disclosed unless (a) the Court otherwise orders, (b) the parties otherwise agree, or (c) otherwise required or permitted by law. (2) For the purposes of subrule (1) the information and records are: (a) information provided or disclosed by one party to another in an affidavit served under this Division; (b) information provided or disclosed by one party to another in a record referred to in an affidavit served under this Division; (c) information recorded in a transcript of questioning made or in answers to written questions given under this Division.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.33:1 Rule 5.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.33. 1. Overview In Kang v. MB, 2019 ABQB 246, 2019 CarswellAlta 1972, Justice Mandziuk said: [139] This Rule codified the common law principle that “the law implies an undertaking that information acquired through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose which is ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit”: Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v Caterpillar Tractor Co (1986), 1986 CanLII 1619 (AB QB), 72 AR 354 at para 2, 14 CPR (3d) 110 (ABQB) per Wachowich J (as he then was); Edmonton (Police Service) v Alberta (Law Enforcement Review Board), 2014 ABCA 267 (CanLII). Questioning is intended to be a broad, open process that allows each party to “obtain as complete a picture of the case as possible” and “[i]n return for this freedom to investigate, an implied obligation of confidentiality has emerged in the case law”: Lac d'Amiante du Québec Ltée v 2858-0702 Québec Inc, [2001] 2 SCR 743, 2001 SCC 5 (CanLII) at para 60. [140] Information acquired during the course of a lawsuit through Questioning, Affidavits of Records and related processes cannot be used in collateral proceedings without agreement, an order or under a rule of law. This does not apply to Questioning on Affidavits, where a transcript is produced and filed, becoming part of the public record. The distinction was summarized by Graesser J in Hall v Willcox, 2011 ABQB 78 (CanLII): 40 Rule 5.33 codifies the common law implied undertaking of confidentiality on testimony and records produced under the compulsion of discovery processes in civil litigation. There is a difference between the confidentiality attaching to records which have been produced and answers to questioning under subdivision 3 of Part 5 of the Rules on the one hand, and cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, or for the purposes of an application under Part 6 of the Rules, on the other. The common law implied undertaking applied to the affidavit of records, records produced, examinations for discovery, undertakings on examinations and records produced arising out of the discovery process. The implied undertaking did not apply to cross-examinations on affidavits, which were treated as being akin to testimony in court to which the open court principle applies. [141] Finally, the Supreme Court of Canada addressed this issue in Juman v Doucette, [2008] 1 SCR 157, 2008 SCC 8 (CanLII), finding that with few exceptions “there are good reasons to support the existence of an implied (or, in reality, a court-imposed) undertaking” (at para 23). The first rationale arises from the purposes of pretrial discovery which allows each side in a lawsuit to obtain information, thus narrowing issues, preventing surprise and facilitating settlement where that is possible. The second rationale flows from the first: 26 A litigant who has some assurance that the documents and answers will not be used for a purpose collateral or ulterior to the proceedings in which they are demanded will be encouraged to provide a more complete and candid discovery. This is of particular interest in an era where documentary production is of a magnitude (“litigation by avalanche”) as often to preclude careful pre-screening by the individuals or corporations making production. 27 For good reason, therefore, the law imposes on the parties to civil litigation an undertaking to the court not to use the documents or answers for any purpose other than securing justice in the civil proceedings in which the answers were compelled (whether or not such documents or answers were in their origin confidential or incriminatory in nature). [142] The Supreme Court then set out the test for waiver of the implied undertaking: “[a]n application to modify or relieve against an implied undertaking requires an applicant to demonstrate to the court on a balance of probabilities the existence of a public interest of greater weight than the values the implied undertaking is designed to protect, namely privacy and the efficient conduct of civil litigation” (at para 32). The Court went on to state that a court may relieve a party from the implied undertaking if it is satisfied that the interest of justice outweighs any prejudice that would result to a party who disclosed evidence (at para 34). Significantly, the Court added that when the material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice is virtually non-existent and the application for waiver will generally be granted (at para 35). The Court stressed that the applicant bears the onus of establishing “a superior public interest in disclosure”, and that an undertaking should “only be set aside in exceptional circumstances” (at para 38). The Court went on to discuss categories of superior public interest that had arisen in the precedents (e.g., statutory exception, public safety concerns, impeaching inconsistent testimony and the suggested “crimes” exception), but stressed that “it is inherent in any balancing exercise that one interest will not always and in every circumstance prevail over other interests” (at para 48). [143] In Iozzo v Weir, 2004 ABQB 259 (CanLII), Slatter J (as he then was), relying on LSI Logic Corp of Canada Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 710 (CanLII), summarized factors to be considered in deciding whether to grant relief from an implied undertaking (at para 9): (a) the importance of maintaining the integrity of the pre-trial disclosure process; (b) the presence of fraud or criminal wrongdoing; (c) whether the information could have been obtained from other sources; (d) whether third parties are involved; (e) whether the new proceedings involve the same or similar parties or issues, and whether they arise out of the same series of events; (f) whether the injustice that might arise from disclosure outweighs the injustice that might arise from enforcing the undertaking … [149] I agree that with the University Defendants' submission that relief from an implied undertaking should be denied where a party, who is seeking relief from an implied undertaking in order to disclose illegal or improper conduct to the applicable authorities, does so for a collateral purpose (ie, the expectation that the disclosure would be of strategic assistance in his or her litigation): Rennick & Di Pinto; Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd v Toh, 2000 ABQB 814 (CanLII); 755568 Ontario Ltd v Linchris Homes Ltd (1990), 1990 CanLII 6665 (ON SC), 1 OR (3d) 649 (OntCt(GenDiv)); Perrin v Beninger, [2004] OJ No 2353 (SCJ); see also Goodman v Rossi (1995), 1995 CanLII 1888 (ON CA), 24 OR (3d) 359 at 374 (OntCA). 2. Cross-Examinations on Affidavit or Statutory Declaration In Hall v. Willcox, 2011 ABQB 78, 2011 CarswellAlta 146, 511 A.R. 139, Graesser, J. considered whether R. 5.33 applies to a cross-examination on either an affidavit or statutory declaration, and concluded that it does not. The question arose in the context of an application to have a judgment debtor declared to be in civil contempt. The judgment debtor had filed an affidavit, and the judgment creditor had cross-examined him on it, and wanted to use that cross-examination in other proceedings. At paragraphs 49–51, his Lordship said: 49 Rule 5.33 codifies the common law implied undertaking of confidentiality on testimony and records produced under the compulsion of discovery processes in civil litigation. There is a difference between the confidentiality attaching to records which have been produced and answers to questioning under subdivision 3 of Part 5 of the Rules on the one hand, and cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, or for the purposes of an application under Part 6 of the Rules, on the other. The common law implied undertaking applied to the affidavit of records, records produced, examinations for discovery, undertakings on examinations and records produced arising out of the discovery process. The implied undertaking did not apply to cross-examinations on affidavits, which were treated as being akin to testimony in court to which the open court principle applies. 50 The new Rules did not change this difference. Because the transcript of Mr. Willcox is of a cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, the transcript is not subject to Rule 5.33. Even though the cross-examination went beyond questioning on the affidavit or statutory declaration and went into issues relevant to the contempt application, that questioning would be akin to questioning under Rule 6.8 (like the old Rule 266 examination). Such questioning would not have been protected by the implied undertaking and is not now protected by R. 5.33. 51 Thus I do not see that Ms. Hall needs court approval, or an order under R. 5.33, to allow use of the transcript in other proceedings. In L. (P.) v. Alberta, 2012 ABQB 309, 2012 CarswellAlta 1001, 529 A.R. 21, 64 Alta. L.R. (5th) 322, Justice Graesser determined that Rule 5.33 is a codification of the common law. At paragraphs 116–118, his Lordship said: 116 As Rule 5.33 is a codification of the common law as it existed in Alberta at the time the new Rules of Court came into force (November 1, 2010) and the rule has no significant differences from the common law, the prior case law on the implied undertaking is relevant to the new Rule. 117 From the case law, I conclude that on an application to lift the implied undertaking: 1. The party seeking to lift it bears the burden to demonstrate through cogent and persuasive reasons that the relief should be granted; 2. The information sought to be used must be relevant and material to the application or action in which it is sought to be used (in other words this should not be a fishing expedition); and 3. To grant the relief sought, the court must conclude that the public interest in seeing justice done in the particular case outweighs the privacy interest of the litigants involved in the other litigation and the integrity of the discovery process. 118 Considerations in determining whether the implied undertaking should be lifted include the presence of fraud or criminal wrongdoing, whether the information could have been obtained from other sources, whether third parties are involved, and whether the new proceedings are connected with the proceedings in which disclosure was made, in the sense that they involve the same or similar parties, the same or similar issues, and arise out of the same series of events (from LSI Logic, supra). 3. Materials from other proceedings In Klein v. Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28, the parties each brought applications regarding their failed domestic relationship. Justice Renke considered this question: “are materials from other proceedings between the parties (whether prior proceedings or the other application) admissible in either application?” His Lordship said: 8 Court Orders, filed affidavits, and cross-examinations on affidavits in an application are matters of public record (if not sealed) and may be referred to in another application. The “implied undertaking” rule does not apply to these materials: [34] It seems to me that it is almost axiomatic that when affidavits are filed with the Court, they are available for all the world to see and to use within the confines of law. Such information should be no less available for lawful use in collateral proceedings. No good reason has been provided why this should not be so. The principles of transparency in legal proceedings and openness of the court record predominate over the interests of confidentiality between the parties in any particular litigation. I conclude that the implied undertaking and the order for confidentiality do not apply to affidavits filed with the Court or evidence from cross-examination on those affidavits: Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v Wenzel, 2007 ABQB 635 at para 34, Greckol J, affd 2008 ABCA 36; see also Floate v Gas Plus Inc, 2015 ABQB 545, Jeffrey J at para 27. Hence, Orders, affidavits, and cross-examinations on affidavits from other proceedings between the parties may be relied on (if otherwise admissible) in either the Family Law Act or Law of Property Act application. (c)—implied undertakings rule 9… Paragraph 5.33(1)(c) (“otherwise … permitted by law”) is engaged as indicated respecting public documents. Regardless, information disclosed in prior litigation between these parties or in one application should be admissible in the other application. I grant leave to introduce the information from prior litigation or the other application despite the implied undertaking rule, on the grounds that the parties are the same (Ms Wolbeck and Mr Klein) and the issues are the same or similar (the nature and legal implications of their cohabitation, with particular reference to the economic sequelae of their relationship). According to Justice Binnie in Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 157 at para 35: • [35] The case law provides some guidance to the exercise of the court's discretion. For example, where discovery material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same or similar parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice to the examinee is virtually non-existent and leave will generally be granted … See also: Perehudoff v Christiano, 2013 ABQB 390, Jones J at paras 22 - 26; ET v Rocky Mountain Play Therapy Institute Inc, 2015 ABQB 396, Mason M; Orlecki v Challenge Insurance Group Inc, 2014 ABQB 664, Schlosser M; PL v Alberta, 2012 ABQB 309, Graesser J at para 117. I should add that preventing information disclosed in other relationship-related litigation between the parties from being relied on in the applications before me would be contrary to the public interest. The ability to hide evidence in plain sight from the other party would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. 4. When the Obligation is Triggered In Novotny v. LePan, 2011 ABQB 205, 2011 CarswellAlta 615, 516 A.R. 69, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 122; additional reasons at 2011 CarswellAlta 969, 2011 ABQB 272, 516 A.R. 76, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 131, Ms. Novotny filed a Statement of Claim naming LePan as defendant. Ms. Novotny sought relief under the Divorce Act and under the Matrimonial Property Act. She subsequently amended the Statement of Claim to add two more defendants (a woman named McCann with whom LePan had formed a new relationship, and her company named FLIPP Advertising Inc.). The same lawyer acted for all three defendants. LePan's counsel made a formal demand of Novotny for certain financial information. Ms. Novotny applied for an order “that would have the effect of preventing counsel for all three of the Defendants from continuing to act for all three.” She submitted that the demand for information was made in the divorce action (to which only LePan was a party), but that since the same lawyer acted for all three defendants, the lawyer he would have to disclose the financial information received to all three defendants. She relied on Rule 8(d) of the Law Society's Code of Professional Conduct which states that “when acting for more than one party in the same matter, a lawyer must disclose to all such parties any material confidential information acquired by the lawyer in the course of the representation and relating to the matter in question.” Ms. Novotny submitted that the lawyer could not comply with that obligation without violating Rule 5.33(1). Justice Jeffrey did not agree, and said, at paragraphs 13-15, and 18-26: 13 In my view the divorce action and the matrimonial property action have not been consolidated. If they were, then I would agree with the Defendants' argument. While headings are rarely determinative, they are often instructive. The heading immediately before Rule 12.9 is “Starting Combined Proceeding”. This suggests a different intent than consolidation and is in keeping with the reasoning in Lord at paras. 27-31. In that decision Chrumka J. stated (at para. 30) that Rule 563 (the predecessor to Rule 12.9) “is a procedural rule which permits two actions to be commenced together but this does not result in those two actions becoming one.” 14 The obligation in Rule 5.33 is triggered when information “for the purpose of carrying on an action” is received. In the context of a combined proceeding, then, involving more than one action, the Rule 5.33 obligation does require a litigant and a counsel, such as the Defendants' counsel here, to not disclose to third parties information received from an adverse party for the purposes of that single action, even when those third parties are involved in some capacity in the combined proceeding. 15 The issue before the Court falls to be determined on the basis of whether the Code obliges Defendants' counsel to breach this implied undertaking and Rule 5.33. ..... 18 Rule 5.33 prohibits LePan and his counsel from disclosing Novotny's confidential information outside the scope and purposes of “the action” for which it was received—in this case the divorce action. Section 8(d) of Chapter 7 of the Code addresses the situation where a counsel acts for more than one party in “the same matter”. If the words “action” and “matter” are synonymous, Defendants' counsel is not at risk of breaching one of his duties merely by complying with the other. 19 Novotny relies on the Black's Law Dictionary definition of “matter”, which she submits should be interpreted as of similar meaning to “cause of action.” She argues that “In the instant case the causes of action, or foundational matters, are overlapping whereas the actions themselves are distinct.” 20 The Defendants rely upon D.R. Devine Roofing & Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Ledcor Construction Ltd. (2007), 51 C.P.C. (6th) 314 (Ont. S.C.J.), where the Defendants submit that the phrases “same matter” and “same dispute” are used interchangeably. The Defendants further submit that the phrase “same matter,” when used in the context of Ch. 7 Rule 8, is synonymous with the phrases “same action,”“same lawsuit” and “same dispute” and thus no issue arises. 21 Although helpful I do not find the guidance provided by the parties determinative. My impression would be that the two are different as Novotny suggests, “matter” having a broader scope than “action”. But I am reluctant to interpret definitively a term of the Code given both the nature of the document as described above and without the benefit of the Law Society of Alberta's representations on the point. Fortunately, for the reasons that follow, it is not necessary for me to do so in the context of this application. I deny the application for the following two reasons. 22 First, the Defendants' counsel's obligation to share information under Ch. 7 Rule 8(d) is triggered only if the information is “material”. If, as Novotny argues, her confidential information in response to the Demand is irrelevant to the claims against McCann and FLIPP, then it is not material to them and need not be disclosed to them pursuant to Ch.7 Rule 8(d). If the information is material, then the information which Defendants' counsel would be professionally obligated to disclose to all clients would be information that McCann and FLIPP would be entitled to receive directly from the disclosing litigant opposite, in the normal course, regardless of who acts for them. 23 It might be argued that by that reasoning I have mistaken “material” for “relevant”. Materiality and relevance are not synonymous but, in the context of the Code at Ch.7 Rule 8(d), in my view the term “material” was intended to entail that the information is also relevant. The Code would not require members to communicate irrelevant information to other unaffected clients simply because it was material simpliciter. Counsel representing a number of plaintiffs as a class comes to mind as but one example. The Code obligation would not extend to require counsel to the class to disclose, say, medical information material to one member of the class, to all members of the class even though irrelevant to the individual legal interests. 24 Therefore, Defendants' counsel does not appear to be required by the Code to disclose Novotny's information that he receives on behalf of LePan in the divorce action to his other clients that he represents in the matrimonial property action. It is not material to them. If it was material to their legal interests within the matrimonial property action, they would be entitled to that information directly from Novotny. Therefore Defendants' counsel will not be placed in the situation of breaching at least one of Rule 5.33 or the Code upon receipt of Novotny's disclosure. 25 Second, the Court is averse to deny a litigant their choice of counsel. See, for example, Alberta (Treasury Branches) v. Leahy, 1998 ABCA 286, 223 A.R. 113. The standard for the removal of counsel is objective and is that of a reasonably informed member of the public: MacDonald Estate at 1259-1260 (majority decision of Sopinka, J.). As stated in Everingham v. Ontario (1992), 8 O.R. (3d) 121 (Div. Ct.) at 127, “[t]he issue is whether a fair-minded reasonably informed member of the public would conclude that the proper administration of justice required the removal of the solicitor.” 26 On this standard, I see no reason to displace the Defendants' choice of counsel. Novotny has not shown how the current multi-party representation offends the administration of justice. She submits that, practically speaking, it would be impossible for the Defendants' counsel to keep her confidential disclosure in the divorce action separate from the disclosure pursuant to the matrimonial property action. I have been given no reason to apprehend that Defendants' counsel shall not abide his professional and legal obligations as conscientiously as any other member of the Law Society of Alberta. A fair-minded reasonably informed member of the public would not conclude that the proper administration of justice required the removal of Defendants' counsel from representing one or some of the Defendants. In MBH v. CKI, 2023 ABKB 284, 2023 CarswellAlta 1221, Justice Marion discussed when the obligations under the Rule are triggered: [70] Rule 5.33 recognizes that many produced records are confidential, and therefore are subject to the implied undertaking that the documents will not be used for collateral purposes: Kaddoura v Hanson, 2015 ABCA 154 at para 31. However, rule 5.33 does not cover all information revealed during litigation; it is limited in its scope to information provided or disclosed under Part 5, Division 1 of the Rules, which relates only to the Part 5 discovery process: Makis v Alberta Health Services, 2020 ABCA 168 at para 61. [71] In the context of family proceedings, rule 5.33 applies to oral questioning for discovery under rule 5.17, and an affidavit of records compelled pursuant to rule 12.38 (since rule 12.38 simply provides a different procedural mechanism to trigger the service of an affidavit of records as delineated in Part 5, Division 1). In my view, rule 5.33 also applies to written interrogatories under rule 12.40 because the rule 12.40 process applies “in place of rule 5.28”, which I interpret to mean that rule 12.40 written interrogatories are effectively given under Part 5, Division 1. However, rule 5.33 does not apply to a notice to disclose documents under 12.41 or a request for financial information under rule 12.42 because those distinct processes are not contemplated in Part 5, Division 1. [72] In my view, the Prescription Records, the Physician Records and the Hospital Records are not captured by rule 5.33 because they were not compelled under Part 5, Division 1 but were produced in the context of a questioning on an affidavit under rule 6.7: Gill v 735458 Alberta Inc, 2003 ABQB 501 at paras 17-34; Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2007 ABQB 635 at paras 30-34; Klein v Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28 at para 8; Terringo v Fox, 2023 ABKB 89 at paras 113-114. [73] However, I find that rule 5.33 does apply to the August 7 Records, which I have ordered to be produced without the need for CKI to formally request an Affidavit of Records. They are akin to compelled Part 5 disclosure. Accordingly, rule 5.33 restricts CKI from using the August 7 Records other than for the purpose of carrying on the action. 5. Application to be relieved from implied undertaking In Kent v. Martin, 2013 ABQB 27, 2013 CarswellAlta 400, 554 A.R. 204, the plaintiff applied for relief from an implied undertaking. In reviewing the law on the topic, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraphs 6–9: 6 While Rule 5.33 now deals explicitly with implied undertakings in Alberta, the leading case dealing with implied undertakings is Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, [2008] 1 SCR 157 [Juman] The principles in Juman have been recently summarized by the B.C. Supreme Court in Henry v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2012 BCSC 1878, as follows: [42] Pursuant to the implied undertaking rule, evidence compelled during pre-trial discovery can be used only for the purpose of the litigation in which it was obtained. The rule applies to both civil and criminal proceedings: R. v. Basi, 2011 BCSC 314. [43] The rule attempts to balance the public interest in getting at the truth against a litigant's privacy interest. To that end a litigant will be compelled to make full disclosure, but the law imposes on the party an undertaking to the court not to use the documents or answers for any purpose other than securing justice in the proceedings in which the answers or documents were compelled: Juman paras. 23–28. [44] The undertaking is not absolute. It may be trumped by a more compelling public interest and a party may apply to the court for leave to use the information or documents other than in the action in which they were disclosed. An application to modify or be relieved against an implied undertaking requires the applicant to demonstrate on a balance of probabilities the existence of a public interest of greater weight than the values that the implied undertaking is designed to protect: Juman, para. 32. [45] In Juman, the court discussed the criteria and factors the court should weigh in determining whether or not to lift an undertaking when an application is made to use material in one action in a different proceeding. The court noted at para. 35 that when discovery material in one action is sought to be used in another action between the same or similar parties and raising the same or similar issues, the prejudice is virtually non-existent and leave will generally be granted. [46] The implied undertaking continues even after the proceeding in which it originated terminates. The undertaking is, however, spent when the documents become part of the court record at trial but not otherwise, except by consent or court order: Juman, para. 51. 7 I believe the above-referenced summary of Juman and new Rule 5.33 apply nicely to the case at bar. In other words: (a) Pre-trial discovery evidence should only be used in the litigation in which it has been obtained, and (b) if there is a more compelling public interest in doing so, a party may ultimately apply to the Court for leave to use that information in the other “proceeding” if the Court believes the applicant has proven on a balance of probabilities the public interest supports it being used there. 8 In short, the implied undertaking is a significant barrier requiring extraordinary caution in the use of disclosed evidence. And as my reasons below point out, relief from the undertaking need not be given if the information underlying the application is already public. 9 The Applicant properly applies for relief from the implied undertaking—an undertaking that I repeat should only be set aside in rare circumstances: Juman, at para 38. This point and a subsequent ruling made by Justice Belzil in an earlier case involving this Plaintiff: (Kent v. Martin, 2010 ABQB 479), 34 Alta LR (5th) 317 speak to this caution. Accordingly, the Applicant followed the proper steps in bringing the matter to the Court. In Secure Energy Services Inc. v. CCS Corp., 2014 ABQB 107, 2014 CarswellAlta 279, 6 Alta. L.R. (6th) 349, Chief Justice Wittmann commented on the rule, and the law governing the lifting of the implied undertaking (at paragraphs 11–13): 11 ARC 5.33 is a codification of what is known as the implied undertaking rule. That rule has long provided that evidence compelled during pre-trial discovery, in the course of civil litigation, may be used by the parties only for the purpose of the litigation in which it was obtained. The scope of the implied undertaking rule was set out by Binnie J. in Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8. at para.4: Thus the rule is that both documentary and oral information obtained on discovery, including information thought by one of the parties to disclose some sort of criminal conduct, is subject to the implied undertaking. It is not to be used by the other parties except for the purpose of that litigation, unless and until the scope of the undertaking is varied by a court order or other judicial order or a situation of immediate and serious danger emerges. 12 In L.(P) v. Alberta, 2012 ABQB 309 Graesser J. rejected an application to lift the implied undertaking with respect to records and information given in questioning in other, similar actions against the province of Alberta. Graesser J. noted that ARC 5.33 effectively codified the implied undertaking at common law and that prior case law in respect of the implied undertaking is relevant to ARC 5.33. After briefly surveying that prior case law, he held, at paras.117-118: From the case law, I conclude that on an application to lift the implied undertaking: 1. The party seeking to lift it bears the burden to demonstrate through cogent and persuasive reasons that the relief should be granted; 2. The information sought to be used must be relevant and material to the application or action in which it is sought to be used (in other words this should not be a fishing expedition); and 3. To grant the relief sought, the court must conclude that the public interest in seeing justice done in the particular case outweighs the privacy interest of the litigants involved in the other litigation and the integrity of the discovery process. Considerations in determining whether the implied undertaking should be lifted include the presence of fraud or criminal wrongdoing, whether the information could have been obtained from other sources, whether third parties are involved, and whether the new proceedings are connected with the proceedings in which disclosure was made, in the sense that they involve the same or similar parties, the same or similar issues, and arise out of the same series of events (from LSI Logic, supra). 13 I agree with the formulation set out by Graesser J. but would add that it is important at every stage to have regard to the heavy burden borne by the applicant, which arises out of the compelling rationale underlying the implied undertaking. The proposition that the applicant bears a heavy burden is well established in Alberta: see LSI Logic Corp. of Canada Inc. v. Logani, 2001 ABQB 710 at para.107, Jutte v. Jutte, 2007 ABQB 191 at para. 26, and L(P), at para.115. The rationale is stated by Binnie, J. in Doucette, at paras.25 - 26: The public interest in getting at the truth in a civil action outweighs the examinee's privacy interest, but the latter is nevertheless entitled to a measure of protection. The answers and documents are compelled by statute solely for the purpose of the civil action and the law thus requires that the invasion of privacy should generally be limited to the level of disclosure necessary to satisfy that purpose and that purpose alone … The general idea, metaphorically speaking, is that whatever is disclosed in the discovery room stays in the discovery room unless eventually revealed in the courtroom or disclosed by judicial order. There is a second rationale supporting the existence of an implied undertaking. A litigant who has some assurance that the documents and answers will not be used for a purpose collateral or ulterior to the proceedings in which they are demanded will be encouraged to provide a more complete and candid discovery. This is of particular interest in an era where documentary production is of a magnitude (“litigation by avalanche”) as often to preclude careful pre-screening by the individuals or corporations making production. Also in Secure Energy Services Inc. v. CCS Corp., the plaintiff had received records from the defendant and wanted to release those records to the Competition Bureau. The application was denied. Chief Justice Wittmann said, at paragraphs 15–18): 15 Secure points to a number of cases in which the implied undertaking has been lifted, allowing for the production of records and information to third party tribunals. These cases are instructive. In S.K v. Lee, [2000] O.J. No. 3423 (SCJ), the Court agreed to lift the implied undertaking so as to allow a physician, facing sexual abuse claims before the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to challenge the credibility and reliability of the complainant. In Engel v. Mehid, 2008 ABQB 608, Moen J lifted the implied undertaking to allow a police officer, facing disciplinary proceedings, to use the complainant's discovery transcripts, from a parallel civil action that had since been discontinued, again primarily for the purpose of challenging the complainant's credibility and reliability in the disciplinary proceeding. In both instances, the courts concluded that the right to a full answer and defence in the context of extremely serious disciplinary proceedings warranted lifting the implied undertaking, under strict conditions. In Engel, because the evidence at issue was contained in the discovery transcripts in the civil proceeding, it could not have been available from any other source. Somewhat similarly, in Kent v. Martin, 2011 ABQB 298, Miller J. allowed the applicant to disclose evidence obtained in the course of examinations for discovery to the Law Society of Alberta, in support of the plaintiff's complaint against his former solicitor. On an earlier application (2010 ABQB 479), Belzil J. had struck the plaintiff's Statement of Claim against the former solicitor, which was based upon the same discovery evidence, on the basis that but for the breach of the implied undertaking, the action could not have been filed. After noting that the application to disclose the evidence to the Law Society of Alberta was unopposed, Miller J. concluded that the public interest in the ethical practice of law outweighed the privacy interests of the solicitor. 16 None of the foregoing decisions speak to the issue here, which is whether the confidentiality imposed by ARC 5.33 should be lifted so as to allow Secure to produce to the Competition Bureau whole volumes of records in the hope of reviving an investigation the Bureau has closed. In Doucette, Binnie J. held, at paras.36-37: On the other hand, courts have generally not favoured attempts to use the discovered material for an extraneous purpose, or for an action wholly unrelated to the purposes of the proceeding in which the discovery was obtained in the absence of some more compelling public interest … Some applications have been refused on the basis that they demonstrate precisely the sort of mischief the implied undertaking rule was designed to avoid. In 755568 Ontario Ltd., for example, the plaintiff sought leave to send the defendant's discovery transcripts to the police. The court concluded that the plaintiff's strategy was to enlist the aid of the police to discover further evidence in support of the plaintiff's claim and/or to pressure the defendant to settle. 17 Secure's professed reason for seeking an order lifting the confidentiality imposed by ARC 5.33 is that it is in the public interest. As stated earlier, there is a public interest in truth seeking in civil litigation. Another competing public interest is embodied in the Competition Act. In s. 1.1 it is stated that the purpose of the Act is to maintain and encourage competition in Canada; a reason articulated, is to promote the efficiency and adaptability of the Canadian economy with the end result to providing consumers with competitive prices and product choice. 18 Although there is no direct evidence that the real reason Secure is bringing the application is to apply pressure on CCS in furtherance of this Action, to allow Secure to provide the Patriot Documents to the Competition Bureau would have that result. That result is precisely what ARC 5.33 is intended to discourage. 6. Implied Undertakings outside R. 5.33 In Floate v. Gas Plus Inc., 2015 ABQB 545, a government agency came into possession of information in the course of its regulatory activities. That government agency later became a party in civil litigation. Justice Jeffrey put the issue this way: These applications address whether the “implied undertaking” not to use information received via discovery in a civil proceeding, except for purposes of that proceeding, applies to the records received by a governmental agency in the course of its regulatory activities, when that governmental agency later finds itself in civil litigation. Justice Jeffrey started his analysis by stating that R. 5.33 did not apply. He then said: 46 Fourth, counsel representing a party in civil litigation bears a professional obligation to, among other things: a. Not make use of records accidentally or improperly obtained: Firemaster Oilfield Services Ltd. v Safety Boss (Canada) (1993) Ltd., 2000 ABQB 932, at para 22, see also rule 6.02(12) of the Alberta Law Society Code of Conduct; b. Not use privileged information adverse to the person who made the confidential communication: Tilley v Hails (1993), 12 OR (3d) 306 (Ont Gen Div), see also rule 2.03(2) of the Alberta Law Society Code of Conduct; and c. Request the character of a record be determined by the court, when unsure whether privilege attaches to it: Firemaster Oilfield Services Ltd. v Safety Boss (Canada) (1993) Ltd., 2001 ABCA 248 at para 7; Miller v Miller, 2000 ABQB 12 at paras 6 & 54. This role of the court is not to be arrogated by counsel: Miller, at para 54 (collectively, “Counsel's Obligations”). 47 Fifth, issues of production and confidentiality during the discovery phase of a civil action are a matter of judicial discretion. The Alberta Court of Appeal said in Husky Oil Operations Limited v Anadarko Canada Corporation, 2004 ABCA 154, at para 8: The granting of an application for production or discovery of documents is a discretionary decision: see, for example, Grain Claims Bureau Ltd. v. Canada Surety Co., [1927] 4 D.L.R. 297 (Man. K.B.); Agala v. Agala, [1998] B.C.J. No. 2827. The granting of a confidentiality order is, similarly, an exercise of judicial discretion: Sierra Club v. Canada (Minister of Finance), [2002] 2 S.C.R. 522. The Implied Undertaking in Other Contexts 48 The implied undertaking prevents litigants from using evidence obtained in compelled pre-trial discovery or disclosure for any collateral purpose, other than the litigation in which it was produced: Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8 at para 1. In that case the Supreme Court of Canada described the rule as follows, at para 4 (emphasis in original): Thus the rule is that both documentary and oral information obtained on discovery, including information thought by one of the parties to disclose some sort of criminal conduct, is subject to the implied undertaking. It is not to be used by the other parties except for the purpose of that litigation, unless and until the scope of the undertaking is varied by a court order or other judicial order or a situation of immediate and serious danger emerges. 49 Once the information is placed on the public record, the implied undertaking no longer applies. In Edmonton (Police Service) v Alberta (Law Enforcement Review Board), 2014 ABCA 267, the Alberta Court of Appeal said, at para 43: […] Typically … the implied undertaking of confidentiality for information disclosed in pre-trial civil litigation disappears if and when the information becomes evidence at trial, as trials are public proceedings. […] Any evidence entered at a trial therefore passes into the public domain. 50 The court explained the purpose of the implied undertaking as follows, at para 34: The purpose of the rule arises from the compelled aspect of discovery evidence—i.e. parties to civil litigation are required to disclose relevant information regardless of privacy concerns and whether or not it tends to self-incriminate. At root is the view that each party will provide more complete discovery if given the assurance that disclosure will not be used for collateral purposes … 51 Courts have had opportunity to consider whether the implied undertaking applies in contexts other than standard civil litigation discovery. It has been applied in public inquiries: see Doucette at para 20, in which the court referred to the inquiry into the Westray Mine tragedy. In concluding that no implied undertaking of confidentiality attached to documents obtained by the regulatory body, Justice Jeffrey said: 76 I conclude that the remainder of the Records in the possession of the Regulators, both the Offence Investigation Records and the Regulatory Activities Records at the heart of the dispute between the Applicants and Respondents, are not subject to any implied undertaking, for the following reasons. 77 First, legislators not the courts control the Regulators' process and there is no statutory, regulatory or “Regulator-specific” practice that imposes an undertaking here. 78 The Regulators are statutory creations; the legislature determines the powers the Regulators require to achieve their statutory mandates. The court is not the master of those regulatory processes in the same way it controls the civil litigation process. The court does not have a comparable responsibility to enhance the effectiveness of those regulatory processes, to accord the Regulators additional tools to achieve their statutory purposes. That is the proper domain of the legislators. The court is independent of such matters and must remain so. The court only supervises regulatory decision-making processes, upon application for judicial review or appeal, to ensure their legality and procedural fairness. 79 At common law, the implied undertaking is an undertaking to the court: Doucette at para 27. I do not consider regulatory investigators or other regulatory agents and employees to owe the court an undertaking of confidentiality over all the information they receive from others—nor should they. It is not the court's place to impose or imply such an undertaking, so that the effectiveness of the various regulatory processes might be improved. It would improperly import the civil litigation duty into an entirely different context. 80 When legislators have wanted to, they have used a range of measures to ensure regulatory bodies receive full information and disclosure. They have granted whistleblower protection to individuals who supply information to a particular regulator.6 They have permitted regulators to grant immunity from enforcement to a polluter who self-reports and cooperates with the regulator to rectify the problem and remediate its effects.7 Legislators sometimes make obstruction an offence and grant powers to search and seize. In addition, they may provide expressly for confidentiality of a record of investigation, as the court noted in Jacques, pursuant to section 29 of the Competition Act. Similarly, in Consolidated NBS Inc, disclosure was ordered subject to the limitations set out in the Ontario Securities Act. Legislators also may dictate the desired degree of transparency or protection of private information in freedom of information and protection of privacy legislation. … 85 The existence of any such express statutory protection or regulator-specific practice is not dispositive of the issue of disclosure in subsequent civil litigation, but its presence or absence will be given considerable weight in the court's exercise of discretion on that question, as the court controls its own process and ensures fairness in each specific proceeding. If, however, after considering the question of the litigants' access to information in the possession of a regulator, the court does order certain information to remain confidential, it will not be the result of any implied undertaking to the court. When the Regulators received the Records in dispute they were not receiving them as part of a civil litigation process, controlled by the court, but as part of an administrative process, that answers to the legislators. In MBH v. CKI, 2023 ABKB 284, 2023 CarswellAlta 1221, Justice Marion said: [76] The implied undertaking does not apply to all information revealed during litigation. For example, it does not cover pleadings, exhibits attached to affidavits by the producing party, or exhibits entered on the court record at trial: Juman at paras 21 and 51; Makis at para 61; Sterr v Merklinger, 1995 CanLII 7134 (ONSC) affirmed 1996 CanLII 10253 (Ont CA); Chevalier v Sunshine Village Corp, 2011 ABQB 557 at paras 6-7; AM Gold Inc v Kaizen Discovery Inc, 2021 BCCA 70 at para 42; Edmonton (Police Service) at para 45. [77] Further, in some circumstances, the undertaking may not protect records or information that a party voluntarily discloses: Hamilton v Alberta (Minister of Public Works, Supply & Services), [1991] 5 WWR 232, 1991 CanLII 5854 (ABKB) at para 28; Chow v Cheung, 2022 BCSC 26 at para 40; Canada v Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236 at paras 14-15; Ibrahim v Lee, 2023 BCSC 28 at para 111; Spiring v Spiring, 2004 MBQB 55 at para 60; K(M) v B(CR), [1996] NWTR 168, 1995 CanLII 18230 (NWTSC) at para 22. [78] In the context of family litigation under Part 12 of the Rules, in my view the implied undertaking rule applies to records and information provided pursuant to Part 5 Discovery, but also other forms in which information is compelled, including information disclosed in response to a Notice to Disclose in Form FL-17 under rule 12.41, or a request for financial information pursuant to sections 65(1) or (4) of the Family Law Act, SA 2003, c F-4.5, as contemplated by rule 12.42. It would also apply to court-ordered disclosure, for example under a Family Docket Court Endorsement. [79] However, in this case, the Disclosed Records were not compelled under Part 5 or pursuant to the other ways to compel records in family litigation. They were produced by way of responses to undertakings given in the context of a questioning on an affidavit under rule 6.7. In this case, MBH simply produced the Disclosed Records without objecting to the undertaking request. While one might argue that this means these records were voluntarily produced and the implied undertaking should not apply, in my view, that would be too restrictive an interpretation of the implied undertaking rule. [80] Once a person files an affidavit, they are subject to questioning on that affidavit and are compelled to answer questions that are relevant and material to the underlying application: rule 6.7; Blough v Busy Music Inc, 2018 ABQB 560 at para 37; Rozak Estate v Demas, 2011 ABQB 239 at para 30. In some cases, as noted earlier, the affiant may be compelled to provide undertaking answers. The fact that a witness produces the requested records without objection or forcing the opposing party to bring an application to compel them does not render them voluntarily produced and without protection of the implied undertaking. In that instance, the information and records are still provided pursuant to a compulsory questioning process. It would undermine the implied undertaking rule and be inconsistent with rule 1.2 of the Rules to require a party to first formally object to gain protection of the implied undertaking, or to refuse the protection of the rule only because the affiant could have actually refused to produce some or all the requested records in the first instance. [81] Accordingly, in my view, records provided as part of undertaking answers on a questioning on an affidavit are subject to the common law implied undertaking rule. There may be limitations on the application of the undertaking, for example where the records become part of the public record. In Simpson v. Pawlowski, 2024 ABCA 254, the Court discussed both the common law implied undertaking of confidentiality and the public record exception: [10] Rule 5.33 codifies the common law principle that “the law implies an undertaking that information acquired through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose which is ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit”: Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v Caterpillar Tractor Company (1986), 1986 CanLII 1619 (AB KB), 43 Alta LR (2d) 299 at para 2, 72 AR 354 (AB QB). [11] The common law principle – known as the implied undertaking of confidentiality - informs the content of the express undertaking of confidentiality created by the Rule. In Lac d’Amiante du Québec Ltée v 2858-0702 Québec Inc, 2001 SCC 51 at paras 78-79, [2001] 2 SCR 743 [Lac d’Amiante], which considered the undertaking of confidentiality applicable under Quebec civil procedure, “the effects of which are analogous to the principles developed by the common law”, the Court held that confidentiality does not apply “to information that is otherwise accessible to the public. If the information is available to the public from other sources, a party should not be given the burden of applying to the court for leave before using it:.”. The information is “held under the direct control of the court and its officers”, becoming part of the public court record as “part of the sitting”, and therefore is available to the public: Lac d’Amiante at paras 66-67. [12] The undertaking of confidentiality therefore does not cover filed affidavits and cross-examination on affidavits that are properly part of the public record (if not sealed). Disclosure is “permitted by law”, as contemplated by Rule 5.33(1)(c), and the affidavit and its exhibits may be used in other proceedings: Klein v Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28 at paras 8-9, 29 Alta LR (6th) 135 [Klein], and citing Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8 at para 35, [2008] 1 SCR 157 [Juman]. Concerns about the confidentiality of disclosed information may be addressed through other mechanisms, such as a restricted court access order under Rules 6.28 to 6.36 or a confidentiality order. [13] The public record exception to the undertaking is consistent with the open court principle. The discovery process is a broad and compulsory search for relevant and material information that facilitates the resolution of the dispute between the parties. “In return for this freedom to investigate, an implied obligation of confidentiality has emerged in the case law…”: Lac d’Amiante at para 60. However, parties who initiate a legal proceeding partially waive their privacy interests. The public’s access to court records generally prevails over the parties’ confidentiality interests in any particular litigation: Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2007 ABQB 635 at paras 31, 34; Gill v 735458 Alberta Inc, 2003 ABQB 501 at paras 25-6, 15 Alta LR (4th) 362; Klein at para 8. This openness ensures that the administration of justice is not impeded by hiding evidence from the court or by inhibiting transparency about court proceedings. [14] The public record exception does not apply where the court record is filed in the previous action for an improper or collateral purpose to circumvent the undertaking of confidentiality: Terrigno v Fox, 2023 ABKB 89 at paras 113-5. Here, the appellant does not assert that the defendants filed the affidavit containing the email in the First Action for any improper or collateral purpose. We therefore need not address the specific circumstances in which the public records exception can be negated by such an abuse of process. Analysis [15] The appellant asserts that the public record exception only operates when the records are produced at trial or affixed to an affidavit filed by the party producing them in the litigation. We disagree. [16] In Lac d’Amiante at paragraphs 66-67, the Supreme Court explained that information obtained prior to trial through the discovery process “may become part of the court record if objections are made and are then argued before the court. In those cases, the portion of the examination on discovery in question is part of the sitting… [and] not subject to the obligation of confidentiality.” Chambers applications to resolve discovery objections therefore engage the exception and draw into the public record the contents of the filed transcripts and affidavits used to resolve the controversy. [17] In Juman, the Supreme Court endorsed the principles in Lac d’Amiante. The appellant suggests that comments in Juman at paragraphs 21 and 51 about the undertaking being spent when discovery answers or documents are incorporated into the court record at trial imply that the undertaking must invariably continue until then, subject only to the parties’ contrary intentions or a court order. We do not read the generalized comments in Juman as a rejection of the earlier commentary and reasoning in Lac d’Amiante about the exception applying to court filings during the intermediate stage between the commencement and the trial of an action. The jurisprudence since Lac d’Amiante and Juman is well-settled to the contrary. Moreover, the appellant concedes that non-parties to the action could access the public records and use them in other litigation; no justification is offered for subjecting a party to a higher standard or for changing the admitted public nature of the documents based on who is trying use them. Such an approach, as noted in Lac d’Amiante, would only impose additional complexity and expense by compelling a party to seek permission from the court to utilize the public record. [18] The appellant also asserts that only the party producing the record may “waive” the undertaking before trial by placing the record on the court file. However, the operation of the exception is not a waiver. The undertaking is simply not operative where a record has been entered properly into the public record. [19] Finally, the appellant contends that the public record exception only operates before trial for records produced under Part 6 of the Rules, which addresses applications to the court generally rather than the discovery process. However, that contention ignores the plain wording of Rules 5.32 and 5.33 which frames the undertaking under “this Division”, meaning Division 1 of Part 5. The public record exception is “permitted by law” under Rule 5.33(1)(c).

sentences.text: Commentary § 5.33:1 Rule 5.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Overview In Kang v.

MB, 2019 ABQB 246, 2019 CarswellAlta 1972, Justice Mandziuk said: [139] This Rule codified the common law principle that “the law implies an undertaking that information acquired through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose which is ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit”: Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v Caterpillar Tractor Co
(1986), 1986 CanLII 1619 (AB QB), 72 AR 354 at para 2, 14 CPR
(3d) 110 (ABQB) per Wachowich J (as he then was); Edmonton (Police Service) v Alberta (Law Enforcement Review Board), 2014 ABCA 267 (CanLII).

Questioning is intended to be a broad, open process that allows each party to “obtain as complete a picture of the case as possible” and “[i]n return for this freedom to investigate, an implied obligation of confidentiality has emerged in the case law”: Lac d'Amiante du Québec Ltée v 2858-0702 Québec Inc, [2001] 2 SCR 743, 2001 SCC 5 (CanLII) at para 60.

[140] Information acquired during the course of a lawsuit through Questioning, Affidavits of Records and related processes cannot be used in collateral proceedings without agreement, an order or under a rule of law.
This does not apply to Questioning on Affidavits, where a transcript is produced and filed, becoming part of the public record.

The distinction was summarized by Graesser J in Hall v Willcox, 2011 ABQB 78 (CanLII): 40 Rule 5.33 codifies the common law implied undertaking of confidentiality on testimony and records produced under the compulsion of discovery processes in civil litigation.

There is a difference between the confidentiality attaching to records which have been produced and answers to questioning under subdivision 3 of Part 5 of the Rules on the one hand, and cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, or for the purposes of an application under Part 6 of the Rules, on the other.

The common law implied undertaking applied to the affidavit of records, records produced, examinations for discovery, undertakings on examinations and records produced arising out of the discovery process.
The implied undertaking did not apply to cross-examinations on affidavits, which were treated as being akin to testimony in court to which the open court principle applies.

[141] Finally, the Supreme Court of Canada addressed this issue in Juman v Doucette, [2008] 1 SCR 157, 2008 SCC 8 (CanLII), finding that with few exceptions “there are good reasons to support the existence of an implied (or, in reality, a court-imposed) undertaking” (at para 23).

The first rationale arises from the purposes of pretrial discovery which allows each side in a lawsuit to obtain information, thus narrowing issues, preventing surprise and facilitating settlement where that is possible.

The second rationale flows from the first: 26 A litigant who has some assurance that the documents and answers will not be used for a purpose collateral or ulterior to the proceedings in which they are demanded will be encouraged to provide a more complete and candid discovery.

This is of particular interest in an era where documentary production is of a magnitude (“litigation by avalanche”) as often to preclude careful pre-screening by the individuals or corporations making production.

27 For good reason, therefore, the law imposes on the parties to civil litigation an undertaking to the court not to use the documents or answers for any purpose other than securing justice in the civil proceedings in which the answers were compelled (whether or not such documents or answers were in their origin confidential or incriminatory in nature).

[142] The Supreme Court then set out the test for waiver of the implied undertaking: “[a]n application to modify or relieve against an implied undertaking requires an applicant to demonstrate to the court on a balance of probabilities the existence of a public interest of greater weight than the values the implied undertaking is designed to protect, namely privacy and the efficient conduct of civil litigation” (at para 32).

The Court went on to state that a court may relieve a party from the implied undertaking if it is satisfied that the interest of justice outweighs any prejudice that would result to a party who disclosed evidence (at para 34).

Significantly, the Court added that when the material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice is virtually non-existent and the application for waiver will generally be granted (at para 35).

The Court stressed that the applicant bears the onus of establishing “a superior public interest in disclosure”, and that an undertaking should “only be set aside in exceptional circumstances” (at para 38).

The Court went on to discuss categories of superior public interest that had arisen in the precedents (e.g., statutory exception, public safety concerns, impeaching inconsistent testimony and the suggested “crimes” exception), but stressed that “it is inherent in any balancing exercise that one interest will not always and in every circumstance prevail over other interests” (at para 48).

[143] In Iozzo v Weir, 2004 ABQB 259 (CanLII), Slatter J (as he then was), relying on LSI Logic Corp of Canada Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 710 (CanLII), summarized factors to be considered in deciding whether to grant relief from an implied undertaking (at para 9):
(a) the importance of maintaining the integrity of the pre-trial disclosure process
(b) the presence of fraud or criminal wrongdoing
(c) whether the information could have been obtained from other sources
(d) whether third parties are involved
(e) whether the new proceedings involve the same or similar parties or issues, and whether they arise out of the same series of events

(f) whether the injustice that might arise from disclosure outweighs the injustice that might arise from enforcing the undertaking … [149] I agree that with the University Defendants' submission that relief from an implied undertaking should be denied where a party, who is seeking relief from an implied undertaking in order to disclose illegal or improper conduct to the applicable authorities, does so for a collateral purpose (ie, the expectation that the disclosure would be of strategic assistance in his or her litigation): Rennick & Di Pinto
Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd v Toh, 2000 ABQB 814 (CanLII); 755568 Ontario Ltd v Linchris Homes Ltd
(3d) 649 (OntCt(GenDiv)); Perrin v Beninger, [2004] OJ No 2353 (SCJ); see also Goodman v Rossi
(3d) 359 at 374 (OntCA).
Cross-Examinations on Affidavit or Statutory Declaration In Hall v.
Willcox, 2011 ABQB 78, 2011 CarswellAlta 146, 511 A.R.
139, Graesser, J. considered whether R.
5.33 applies to a cross-examination on either an affidavit or statutory declaration, and concluded that it does not.
The question arose in the context of an application to have a judgment debtor declared to be in civil contempt.
The judgment debtor had filed an affidavit, and the judgment creditor had cross-examined him on it, and wanted to use that cross-examination in other proceedings.

At paragraphs 49–51, his Lordship said: 49 Rule 5.33 codifies the common law implied undertaking of confidentiality on testimony and records produced under the compulsion of discovery processes in civil litigation.

There is a difference between the confidentiality attaching to records which have been produced and answers to questioning under subdivision 3 of Part 5 of the Rules on the one hand, and cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, or for the purposes of an application under Part 6 of the Rules, on the other.

The common law implied undertaking applied to the affidavit of records, records produced, examinations for discovery, undertakings on examinations and records produced arising out of the discovery process.
The implied undertaking did not apply to cross-examinations on affidavits, which were treated as being akin to testimony in court to which the open court principle applies.
50 The new Rules did not change this difference.
Because the transcript of Mr.
Willcox is of a cross-examination on an affidavit or statutory declaration, the transcript is not subject to Rule 5.33.

Even though the cross-examination went beyond questioning on the affidavit or statutory declaration and went into issues relevant to the contempt application, that questioning would be akin to questioning under Rule 6.8 (like the old Rule 266 examination).
Such questioning would not have been protected by the implied undertaking and is not now protected by R.
51 Thus I do not see that Ms.
Hall needs court approval, or an order under R.
5.33, to allow use of the transcript in other proceedings.
In L.
Alberta, 2012 ABQB 309, 2012 CarswellAlta 1001, 529 A.R.
21, 64 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 322, Justice Graesser determined that Rule 5.33 is a codification of the common law.

At paragraphs 116–118, his Lordship said: 116 As Rule 5.33 is a codification of the common law as it existed in Alberta at the time the new Rules of Court came into force (November 1, 2010) and the rule has no significant differences from the common law, the prior case law on the implied undertaking is relevant to the new Rule.
117 From the case law, I conclude that on an application to lift the implied undertaking: 1.
The party seeking to lift it bears the burden to demonstrate through cogent and persuasive reasons that the relief should be granted; 2.
The information sought to be used must be relevant and material to the application or action in which it is sought to be used (in other words this should not be a fishing expedition); and 3.

To grant the relief sought, the court must conclude that the public interest in seeing justice done in the particular case outweighs the privacy interest of the litigants involved in the other litigation and the integrity of the discovery process.

118 Considerations in determining whether the implied undertaking should be lifted include the presence of fraud or criminal wrongdoing, whether the information could have been obtained from other sources, whether third parties are involved, and whether the new proceedings are connected with the proceedings in which disclosure was made, in the sense that they involve the same or similar parties, the same or similar issues, and arise out of the same series of events (from LSI Logic, supra).
Materials from other proceedings In Klein v.
Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28, the parties each brought applications regarding their failed domestic relationship.

Justice Renke considered this question: “are materials from other proceedings between the parties (whether prior proceedings or the other application) admissible in either application?” His Lordship said: 8 Court Orders, filed affidavits, and cross-examinations on affidavits in an application are matters of public record (if not sealed) and may be referred to in another application.

The “implied undertaking” rule does not apply to these materials: [34] It seems to me that it is almost axiomatic that when affidavits are filed with the Court, they are available for all the world to see and to use within the confines of law.
Such information should be no less available for lawful use in collateral proceedings.
No good reason has been provided why this should not be so.
The principles of transparency in legal proceedings and openness of the court record predominate over the interests of confidentiality between the parties in any particular litigation.

I conclude that the implied undertaking and the order for confidentiality do not apply to affidavits filed with the Court or evidence from cross-examination on those affidavits: Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v Wenzel, 2007 ABQB 635 at para 34, Greckol J, affd 2008 ABCA 36; see also Floate v Gas Plus Inc, 2015 ABQB 545, Jeffrey J at para 27.

Hence, Orders, affidavits, and cross-examinations on affidavits from other proceedings between the parties may be relied on (if otherwise admissible) in either the Family Law Act or Law of Property Act application.
(c)—implied undertakings rule 9… Paragraph 5.33(1)(c) (“otherwise … permitted by law”) is engaged as indicated respecting public documents.
Regardless, information disclosed in prior litigation between these parties or in one application should be admissible in the other application.

I grant leave to introduce the information from prior litigation or the other application despite the implied undertaking rule, on the grounds that the parties are the same (Ms Wolbeck and Mr Klein) and the issues are the same or similar (the nature and legal implications of their cohabitation, with particular reference to the economic sequelae of their relationship).
According to Justice Binnie in Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, [2008] 1 S.C.R.
157 at para 35: • [35] The case law provides some guidance to the exercise of the court's discretion.

For example, where discovery material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same or similar parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice to the examinee is virtually non-existent and leave will generally be granted … See also: Perehudoff v Christiano, 2013 ABQB 390, Jones J at paras 22 - 26
ET v Rocky Mountain Play Therapy Institute Inc, 2015 ABQB 396, Mason M
Orlecki v Challenge Insurance Group Inc, 2014 ABQB 664, Schlosser M
PL v Alberta, 2012 ABQB 309, Graesser J at para 117.

I should add that preventing information disclosed in other relationship-related litigation between the parties from being relied on in the applications before me would be contrary to the public interest.
The ability to hide evidence in plain sight from the other party would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
When the Obligation is Triggered In Novotny v.
LePan, 2011 ABQB 205, 2011 CarswellAlta 615, 516 A.R.
69, 50 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 122; additional reasons at 2011 CarswellAlta 969, 2011 ABQB 272, 516 A.R.
76, 50 Alta.
L.R.
Novotny filed a Statement of Claim naming LePan as defendant.
Ms.
Novotny sought relief under the Divorce Act and under the Matrimonial Property Act.
She subsequently amended the Statement of Claim to add two more defendants (a woman named McCann with whom LePan had formed a new relationship, and her company named FLIPP Advertising Inc.).
The same lawyer acted for all three defendants.
LePan's counsel made a formal demand of Novotny for certain financial information.
Ms.

The Implied Undertaking in Other Contexts 48 The implied undertaking prevents litigants from using evidence obtained in compelled pre-trial discovery or disclosure for any collateral purpose, other than the litigation in which it was produced: Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8 at para 1.

In that case the Supreme Court of Canada described the rule as follows, at para 4 (emphasis in original): Thus the rule is that both documentary and oral information obtained on discovery, including information thought by one of the parties to disclose some sort of criminal conduct, is subject to the implied undertaking.

It is not to be used by the other parties except for the purpose of that litigation, unless and until the scope of the undertaking is varied by a court order or other judicial order or a situation of immediate and serious danger emerges.
49 Once the information is placed on the public record, the implied undertaking no longer applies.

In Edmonton (Police Service) v Alberta (Law Enforcement Review Board), 2014 ABCA 267, the Alberta Court of Appeal said, at para 43: […] Typically … the implied undertaking of confidentiality for information disclosed in pre-trial civil litigation disappears if and when the information becomes evidence at trial, as trials are public proceedings.
[…] Any evidence entered at a trial therefore passes into the public domain.

50 The court explained the purpose of the implied undertaking as follows, at para 34: The purpose of the rule arises from the compelled aspect of discovery evidence—i.e. parties to civil litigation are required to disclose relevant information regardless of privacy concerns and whether or not it tends to self-incriminate.

At root is the view that each party will provide more complete discovery if given the assurance that disclosure will not be used for collateral purposes … 51 Courts have had opportunity to consider whether the implied undertaking applies in contexts other than standard civil litigation discovery.
It has been applied in public inquiries: see Doucette at para 20, in which the court referred to the inquiry into the Westray Mine tragedy.

77 First, legislators not the courts control the Regulators' process and there is no statutory, regulatory or “Regulator-specific” practice that imposes an undertaking here.
78 The Regulators are statutory creations; the legislature determines the powers the Regulators require to achieve their statutory mandates.
The court is not the master of those regulatory processes in the same way it controls the civil litigation process.
The court does not have a comparable responsibility to enhance the effectiveness of those regulatory processes, to accord the Regulators additional tools to achieve their statutory purposes.
That is the proper domain of the legislators.
The court is independent of such matters and must remain so.
The court only supervises regulatory decision-making processes, upon application for judicial review or appeal, to ensure their legality and procedural fairness.
79 At common law, the implied undertaking is an undertaking to the court: Doucette at para 27.

I do not consider regulatory investigators or other regulatory agents and employees to owe the court an undertaking of confidentiality over all the information they receive from others—nor should they.
It is not the court's place to impose or imply such an undertaking, so that the effectiveness of the various regulatory processes might be improved.

Blough v Busy Music Inc, 2018 ABQB 560 at para 37

In that instance, the information and records are still provided pursuant to a compulsory questioning process.

The discovery process is a broad and compulsory search for relevant and material information that facilitates the resolution of the dispute between the parties. “In return for this freedom to investigate, an implied obligation of confidentiality has emerged in the case law…”: Lac d’Amiante at para 60.

Gill v 735458 Alberta Inc, 2003 ABQB 501 at paras 25-6, 15 Alta LR
(4th) 362; Klein at para 8.
This openness ensures that the administration of justice is not impeded by hiding evidence from the court or by inhibiting transparency about court proceedings.

[14] The public record exception does not apply where the court record is filed in the previous action for an improper or collateral purpose to circumvent the undertaking of confidentiality: Terrigno v Fox, 2023 ABKB 89 at paras 113-5.
Here, the appellant does not assert that the defendants filed the affidavit containing the email in the First Action for any improper or collateral purpose.
We therefore need not address the specific circumstances in which the public records exception can be negated by such an abuse of process.

Analysis [15] The appellant asserts that the public record exception only operates when the records are produced at trial or affixed to an affidavit filed by the party producing them in the litigation.
We disagree.

[16] In Lac d’Amiante at paragraphs 66-67, the Supreme Court explained that information obtained prior to trial through the discovery process “may become part of the court record if objections are made and are then argued before the court.

In those cases, the portion of the examination on discovery in question is part of the sitting… [and] not subject to the obligation of confidentiality.” Chambers applications to resolve discovery objections therefore engage the exception and draw into the public record the contents of the filed transcripts and affidavits used to resolve the controversy.
[17] In Juman, the Supreme Court endorsed the principles in Lac d’Amiante.

The appellant suggests that comments in Juman at paragraphs 21 and 51 about the undertaking being spent when discovery answers or documents are incorporated into the court record at trial imply that the undertaking must invariably continue until then, subject only to the parties’ contrary intentions or a court order.

We do not read the generalized comments in Juman as a rejection of the earlier commentary and reasoning in Lac d’Amiante about the exception applying to court filings during the intermediate stage between the commencement and the trial of an action.
The jurisprudence since Lac d’Amiante and Juman is well-settled to the contrary.

Moreover, the appellant concedes that non-parties to the action could access the public records and use them in other litigation; no justification is offered for subjecting a party to a higher standard or for changing the admitted public nature of the documents based on who is trying use them.
Such an approach, as noted in Lac d’Amiante, would only impose additional complexity and expense by compelling a party to seek permission from the court to utilize the public record.
[18] The appellant also asserts that only the party producing the record may “waive” the undertaking before trial by placing the record on the court file.
However, the operation of the exception is not a waiver.
The undertaking is simply not operative where a record has been entered properly into the public record.

[19] Finally, the appellant contends that the public record exception only operates before trial for records produced under Part 6 of the Rules, which addresses applications to the court generally rather than the discovery process.
However, that contention ignores the plain wording of Rules 5.32 and 5.33 which frames the undertaking under “this Division”, meaning Division 1 of Part 5.
The public record exception is “permitted by law” under Rule 5.33(1)(c).
