paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.34:1 Rule 5.34 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.34. 1. Does R. 5.34 Apply If Defendant Noted In Default? In Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 457, 2008 CarswellAlta 1001, 455 A.R. 143, 94 Alta. L.R. (4th) 163, the plaintiffs filed and served (pursuant to an order for service ex juris) a statement of claim on the defendants. The defendants were noted in default when they failed to file a statement of defence or a demand of notice. Even so, the plaintiffs served the defendants with a copy of the certificate of readiness which indicated the date for the trial on the assessment of damages. The plaintiffs relied on expert reports in proving damages, but copies of those reports were not served on the defendants (as normally required by Rule 218.1). The issue was whether Rule 218.1 had to be complied with when the defendant, pursuant to Rule 144, was not entitled to notice of proceedings. Yamauchi, J. concluded (at p. 169) that “Rule 144 is intended to govern notwithstanding the apparent obligatory nature of Rule 218.1.” At p. 172, his Lordship said: 23 In this case, Rule 144 is paramount and the Plaintiff did not have to serve the experts' reports on the Defendants pursuant to Rule 218.1. The Defendants showed no interest in the proceedings as they failed to file a statement of defence or demand of notice. The Plaintiff complied with Rule 152, so the Defendants knew that the Plaintiff was proceeding with a trial to determine the assessment of damages, but chose not to participate. Accordingly, they could not be “surprised” by the expert testimony. 24 To require the Plaintiff to comply with Rules 218.1 in this case would make Rule 152 meaningless. Accordingly, in this case, the conflict between Rules 144 and 218.1 must be resolved in favour of the Plaintiff. 2. Contents of Experts' Statement It is my opinion that the term “… the substance of his opinion” in R. 218.1(1) is broad enough to include and is intended to include not only the opinion but the factual information upon which that opinion is based. The factual information should be specific enough to support the conclusion. It should be stated in much the same way as the witness's opinion will be expressed to the court when he gives his evidence. Commonwealth Construction Co. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd. (1985), 40 Alta. L.R. (2d) 89 (Q.B.), at 93, per Purvis J. A consultation report following a preliminary examination of a patient and forming part of a hospital's records does not constitute an expert report within the meaning of R. 218.1: see Dezwart v. Misericordia Hospital (1988), 64 Alta. L.R. (2d) 72 (Q.B.). If, through a witness, one is putting forward “ordinary custom”, the rule must be followed. … where evidence based upon the custom or usage in the trade is led, compliance with rule 218.1 is required. Armstrong v. Foxridge Homes Ltd. (1993), 136 A.R. 243 (Q.B.), at 246, per Montgomery J. In Hennig v. Cox (1998), 66 Alta. L.R. (3d) 358 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Nash had before her an application to exclude from evidence certain R. 218.1(1) statements because they did not comply with the rules (i.e., they did not contain the substance of the opinion of the witness). The respondent (plaintiff) submitted that the witnesses were treating physicians, and that no opinion would be sought from them at trial. In granting the application to exclude all but one of the statements, Her Ladyship said, at pp. 362-63: The Plaintiff argued that some of the witnesses will not be asked for an opinion as to causation or liability. If that is the case, then I agree that compliance with R. 218.1(1) is not required. However, in the application before me, all of the medical witnesses have purported to produce a R. 218.1(1) Statement resulting in the inference that they will, at trial, be asked to state an opinion and the basis of that opinion. The purpose of the Rule is to disclose to opposing counsel the substance and the basis of an expert's opinion. The R. 218.1(1) Statement should provide that information. Once there has been compliance with R. 218.1(1), the Applicant is entitled to assume that the witness will provide an opinion. In my view the opinion and the facts upon which the opinion is based should be clearly stated and capable of discernment from a reading of the R. 218.1(1) Statement. If there are several opinions, then those should be readily ascertainable, together with the facts upon which the opinions are based. I don't think that it is incumbent upon counsel for the Applicants to have to guess whether there is an opinion contained in the material submitted and then have to try to determine the facts upon which the opinion is based. I am mindful that the members of the medical profession do not have legal training. However, I do not think that legal expertise is necessary. R. 218.1 requires that the expert state his opinion and the factual basis for the opinion. That, in my view, is not an onerous or difficult requirement. If the medical reports, test results, medical records and letters to the referring physicians do not contain that information, then a further document is required wherein the expert states his opinion and the factual basis for that opinion. The cases establish that the rule should be interpreted so as to promote pretrial disclosure and not to frustrate it. 3. Method of Providing Information under the Rule In Clark v. Rocky View No. 44 (Municipal District) (1995), 37 C.P.C. (3d) 1 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Wilkins considered an application to exclude from evidence the opinions of three medical experts due to an alleged failure to comply with R. 218.1. The plaintiff, who wished to call the experts at trial, had provided to the defendants the information he had received from the experts. All but two reports and curricula vitae were provided more than 90 days prior to trial. At pp. 3-5 his Lordship said: There is no dispute that the plaintiff has provided counsel for the defendant all the medical information received from Dr. Goddard, Dr. Filipchuk and Dr. Davis together with access to their complete medical files in response to discovery undertakings. With the exception of a report and curriculum vitae dated March 29, 1995 (Dr. Davis) and a report and curriculum vitae for Dr. Filipchuk dated March 15, 1995 all of that medical evidence was provided more than 90 days before the trial… I have reviewed the medical information provided by the plaintiff to the defendant. It is my opinion that that information so provided is sufficient compliance with the rule to permit the exercise of my discretion to grant leave to the plaintiff to call the expert witnesses being the three doctors identified in the certificate of readiness and at the pre-trial conference. The defendant complains that service of medical information in compliance with the rule requires at least a cover letter indicating its service pursuant to the rule. I cannot accept such an argument. Surely the rule is designed to provide the defendant with access to the relevant medical information for purpose of knowing the case the defendant faces. If the defendant has, by means of discovery and undertakings given, received the medical evidence including correspondences and opinion letters between the doctors, with supporting test results, and copies of medical legal reports directed to counsel within the time period provided in the rule, I do not believe the rule requires a further encapsulated statement expressly delivered with reference to the rule. In its brief, the defendant cited the decision of Purvis J. in the Commonwealth Construction decision [Commonwealth Construction Co. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd. (1985), 64 A.R. 132 (Q.B.)] as authority for the purposes of the rule. I agree with the analysis of those purposes in that case and the subsequent acknowledgement of those purposes by Rooke J. in his decision in the Kashuba and Guarantee Co. of North America cases… I am also of the view that some additional portions of the judgment of Purvis J. are correct and have direct application to the present case. He states at p. 133 of the decision reported at (1985), 64 A.R. 132 (Q.B.): … I propose to accord to Rule 218.1(1) a large and liberal interpretation. What is the mischief to be suppressed and the remedy effected by this rule? The rule was formulated for the purposes of preventing disruption of the trial process which occurs when litigants are taken by surprise. If parties know ahead of time what expert opinions they will encounter they can adjust to meet the evidence without asking for adjournment. In some cases settlement might be encouraged. In any event, costs and time will be saved and the judicial process will be simplified if there is full disclosure. In cases where the expert's opinion is reduced to writing, it seems that the rule can be most effectively complied with by delivering a copy of the full report to opposing counsel. Copies of the medical reports of each of the three expert witnesses, identifying themselves and signed by them and offering their opinions as the condition of the plaintiff while under treatment were given to counsel for the defendant well before the time required by the rule. In my opinion, any failure to provide a full curriculum vitae for Dr. Filipchuk and Dr. Davis until March 1995 cannot amount to failure to comply with the rule. The further reports of Dr. Filipchuk and Dr. Davis in March 1995 represent updates of medical information previously provided. This information was provided at least two full months before the trial. I would exercise my judicial discretion to allow the expert evidence at trial in relation to the contents of those reports as well… The rule does not require provision of the complete medical evidence that will be given at the trial by the experts but attempts to alert the other party in a timely fashion of the “substance” of that expert evidence. Surely provision in this case of the complete medical reports, test results and medical records goes beyond the rule requirements to permit the defendant an even greater opportunity to rebut or prepare its case on the medical aspects of the case. 4. Conditions Placed on Experts It was held in Big Country Gas Co-op Ltd. v. Plastex Pipeline Systems Ltd. (1986), 44 Alta. L.R. (2d) 338 (Q.B.), that the defendant was not required to disclose, in an examination for discovery, secret manufacturing processes until two plaintiffs gave an undertaking not to disclose such information to anyone except experts not associated with the defendant's competitors or experts approved by the defendants, and any such expert was to file an undertaking of non-disclosure.

paragraphs.text: 5.35. Sequence of exchange of experts' reports
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Sequence of exchange of experts' reports

paragraphs.text: (1) If a party intends to use the evidence of an expert at trial, the expert's report must be served in the sequence described in subrule (2). (2) Unless the parties otherwise agree or the Court otherwise orders, experts' reports on which a party intends to rely must be served in the following sequence: (a) the party who bears the primary onus of proof must serve on each of the other parties the report of that party's expert; (b) the other party or parties must serve their expert's rebuttal report, if any, and may include in the report issues not raised in the initial expert's report; (c) the party who served the initial expert's report may serve a surrebuttal expert's report that responds only to the new issues raised in the rebuttal report.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.35:1 Rule 5.35 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.35. 1. No Formal Notice of Intention Required No formal notice of intention to call a witness is necessary. However, I ruled, distinguishing the situation from Dezwart v. Misericordia Hospital et al. (1988), 96 A.R. 183 (Q.B.)—Hutchinson, J.), that the service of the four reports, while in some way technically in breach of rule 218.1(1), was in substantial compliance with the rule so as to constitute each as a statement under rule 218.1(1). In the process of making that ruling, I ruled (relying by analogy on Fistravec v. Golofinopoulos (1985), 50 C.P.C. 25 (B.C. C.A.)) that there was no actual requirement under rule 218.1(1) that formal notice of an intention to call an expert be given, although that would appear to be the intent of the rule, and therefore, as long as a statement was provided with the requisite information, which, in substance, I found that four reports did, rule 218.1(1) had been complied with. Jivraj v. Fischer (1992), 124 A.R. 81 (Q.B.), at 118-19, per Rooke J. 2. Rebuttal Report In Wade v. Baxter, 2001 ABQB 812, 2001 CarswellAlta 1688, 302 A.R. 1, 98 Alta. L.R. (3d) 230, Slatter J., at p. 251, commented on the contents of a rebuttal report: … a rebuttal report is not confined to merely commenting on the primary reports. A rebuttal report can fairly comment on the theories of the primary report, and provide competing theories to explain the phenomena in issue. It is never very convincing or helpful for an expert to say “I disagree with that theory, but I have no competing theory to offer”. This is particularly so where the expert takes a confession and avoidance approach, as happened when Dr. Glasgow [the Defendant's expert] admitted that the Plaintiff had a serious knee injury, but suggested a competing treatment that might alleviate her symptoms. 3. Surrebuttal Reports In Signalta Resources Limited v. Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2018 ABQB 904, 2018 CarswellAlta 2554, Justice Eamon discussed surrebuttal reports: [7] The content of surrebuttal reports is governed by Rule 5.35(2)(c) of the Alberta Rules of Court… [9] R 5.35 arose from the Alberta Law Reform Institute's recommendation that expert reports be exchanged sequentially … … [11] R 5.35(2)(c) is not limited to alternative theories advanced in a rebuttal report. It refers to a new issue. In my view, this formulation is analogous to the rules respecting rebuttal cases. Lederman, Bryant and Fuerst, The Law of Evidence in Canada (4th ed, 2014) at para 16.211 describe this rule: At the close of the defendant's case, the plaintiff … has the right to adduce rebuttal evidence to contradict or qualify new fact issues raised in defence. The general rule in civil cases is that matters which might properly be considered to form part of the plaintiff's case in chief are excluded … [12] A surrebuttal report must not become a means for a party to split disclosure of its case or to merely confirm or reinforce earlier evidence in its primary expert reports. As with presentation of a case at trial, there is a duty (paraphrasing from the language in Broda v Broda, 2001 ABCA 151 (CanLII) at para 6) to use due diligence to put all one's case in at one time and not split it. As observed in Allcock Laight & Westwood Ltd v Patten, [1967] 1 OR 18, 1966 CanLII 282 (CA) at pp 21-22: It is well settled that where there is a single issue only to be tried, the party beginning must exhaust his evidence in the first instance and may not split his case by first relying on prima facie proof, and when this has been shaken by his adversary, adducing confirmatory evidence: Jacobs v. Tarleton (1848), 11 Q.B. 421, 116 E.R. 534. That case was considered by this Court and the principle therein enunciated was applied in R. v. Michael, 1954 CanLII 101 (ON CA), [1954] O.R. 926, 110 C.C.C. 30, 20 C.R. 18. The rule is now so well settled that it requires no further elaboration. It is important in the trial of actions, whether before a jury or a Judge alone, that this rule should be observed. A defendant is entitled to know the case which he has to meet when he presents his defence and it is not open to a plaintiff under the guise of replying to reconfirm the case which he was required to make out in the first instance or take the risk of non-persuasion. [13] Similar considerations apply to Rule 5.35. It is meant to avoid surprise and encourage parties to ensure that their expert has provided adequate disclosure of the substance of his or her opinion in its primary report. It should also be applied, like the rule against case splitting, to avoid “the interminable confusion that would be created by an unending alternation of successive fragments of each case which could have been put in at once in the beginning” (Wigmore, Evidence (Chadbourn rev, 1976), § 1873, p 672). [14] There may in some cases be a fine line between matters which are merely confirmatory and those adduced to meet new issues. Wigmore (ibid at p 672) states: … Everything relevant as part of the case in chief would naturally have already been put in; and a rebuttal is necessary only because, on a plea in denial, new subordinate evidential facts have been offered or because, on an affirmative plea, its substantive facts have been put forward or because, on any issue whatever, facts discrediting the proponent's witnesses have been offered. To discriminate between the first of these classes and the opponent's testimony merely denying the same facts that the proponent's witness had originally affirmed, is no doubt often difficult, and it is then not easy to say whether the proponent's testimony in rebuttal might or might not as well have been put in originally; yet the principle involved is clear … An example offered by Wigmore is the case of evidence offered to impeach the opponent's witness, for example by way of bias, self-contradiction or the like (ibid at pp 678-679). [15] The purpose of the expert report process is to encourage meaningful pre-trial disclosure and help focus the issues. The Rule should not be applied so rigidly as to force a party tendering a primary report to speculate about what a rebuttal report might contain, or advance excessive commentary and information simply to avoid arguments that it is case splitting. There may be a fine line between matters which are merely confirmatory and those which genuinely arise from some alternative theory or new dimension raised in the opposition's rebuttal report. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.37(2):1 Rule 5.37(2) See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.37(2). What is included in the term “expert's report”? In B.J.M. v. S.L.M., 2012 ABQB 731, Madam Justice Phillips said, at paragraphs 36-37: 36 In my view, the documents reviewed by Dr. Pezzot-Pearce in preparing the Pezzot-Pearce Report must be disclosed and the questioning may address those documents as well as the Pezzot-Pearce Report itself. The documents to be produced include statements from parties and other witnesses, test results and so on. I have arrived at this conclusion for a number of reasons. First, I am of the opinion that the reference to the expert's report in Rule 5.37(2), and for that matter in Rule 6.42, should be interpreted to include both the report itself and the basis thereof, namely the documents reviewed in preparing it. Without those documents, the questioning of the expert would be of limited utility, particularly in a case like this where the credibility of the expert and the validity of his or her opinion is so crucial to the resolution of the issues. In the absence of the reviewed documentation, counsel's ability to make a meaningful assessment of the expert's opinion would be sharply curtailed and the potential for reduction in trial time and complexity would be lost. In some cases, there may be good reason to limit production of the reviewed documents; this can be achieved through the imposition of conditions pursuant to Rule 5.37(3). This, however, is not such a case. 37 I hasten to add that this interpretation of Rule 5.37(2) does not render it meaningless as there are still other documents that need not be produced and may not be questioned upon. In Ramirez, Mr. Justice Macklin, citing Chernetz, referred to such documents in para. 12 as “working papers”, which he interpreted to include “any communications, memoranda, calculations, notes, diagrams or doodles and preliminary opinions”. Any such working documents in this case are not subject to disclosure or questioning at this time, whether Rule 5.37(2) or Rule 6.42 is in play.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.37(4):1 Rule 5.37(4) See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.37(4). In B.J.M. v. S.J.M., 2012 ABQB 731, Madam Justice Phillips said, at paragraphs 40–44: 40 The remaining question is the proper treatment of Dr. Pezzot-Pearce's evidence given under questioning. As noted above, counsel for Mr. referred to Rule 5.37(4) and asserted that this evidence “would be some evidence of the party who intends to rely on the expert's report and would not be binding upon that party”. 41 Rule 5.37(4) provides that “Evidence of an expert under this Division is to be treated as if it were evidence of an employee of the party who intends to rely on the expert's report.” It appears to have its genesis in the old Rule 200 and the reference thereto in the old Rule 218.8(1), as set out above. 42 The reference to treatment of evidence as if it were that of an employee pertains to the distinction under the old Rules of Court between examination for discovery of a selected officer of a corporation under Rule 214 and of an employee under Rule 200. The substance of the distinction was that evidence given by an officer under Rule 214 was binding upon the corporation, while evidence given by an employee under Rule 200 was not and could be refuted with other evidence. This was succinctly summarized by Mr. Justice Slatter, then of this Court, in Prairie Land Corp. v. Concert Properties Ltd., 2004 ABQB 726, 364 AR 283 at para. 6: The general rule is that the parties to litigation are entitled to examine each other for discovery: Rule 200. As a general rule, non-parties to the action are not subject to discovery. Where one of the parties is a corporation, the examination for discovery has two aspects to it. The corporation is required to nominate a spokesperson whose answers are binding on the corporation: Rule 214(1). In addition, Rule 200 provides that adverse parties can examine “officers or employees” of the corporation, although the answers of the officers and employees cannot be read in evidence against the corporation. 43 In addition, these very useful comments were made by Madam Justice Greckol of this Court in Abramski v. TD Waterhouse Canada Inc., 2006 ABQB 942, 410 A.R. 158 at paras. 21–24: It is true that a corporate party must acknowledge evidence from the examination for discovery of true employees examined pursuant to Rule 200(1)(c) as part of the information of the corporate defendant. … As argued by the Applicant, the practical effect of a corporate acknowledgement in relation to the evidence of an employee is that the evidence may then be read in at trial by the opposite party. That evidence does not bind the corporation, which may still adduce contrary or supplemental information at trial. … The authorities that hold that a corporate party must acknowledge evidence by the examination for discovery of its employees is found in three decisions given by Wachowich C.J. in the same case of Esso Resources Canada v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. In the first decision, [1992] A.J. No. 1204 … Wachowich C.J. explained that a corporation has no personal knowledge or information, rather its knowledge and information is the totality of knowledge and information of its agents, servants, employees and former employees, and there are only limited circumstances under which a corporate officer can refuse to accept an employee's evidence as information of the corporation. While the employee's evidence may form part of the information of the corporation at trial, it is not binding on the corporation, nor is it conclusive or incontrovertible and cannot form the basis of an admission of fact under Rule 230. 44 Applying this analysis to the case before me, I take Rule 5.37(4) to mean that the evidence given by an expert in pre-trial questioning does not bind a party who chooses to call that expert as a witness at trial. Rather, that party would be free to introduce contrary evidence. Normally, of course, an expert will be called as a witness at trial by the party who hired him or her. In this case, as Dr. Pezzot-Pearce was appointed by the Court, she may be called as a witness at trial by either party, but her evidence at questioning will not bind either party.

paragraphs.text: 5.38. Continuing obligation on expert
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Continuing obligation on expert

paragraphs.text: If, after an expert's report has been provided by one party to another, the expert changes his or her opinion on a matter in the report, the change of opinion must be (a) disclosed by the expert in writing, and (b) immediately served on each of the other parties.

paragraphs.text: 5.39. Use of expert's report at trial without expert
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Use of expert's report at trial without expert

paragraphs.text: (1) A party serving an expert's report may, at the same time, also serve notice of intention to have the report entered as evidence without calling the expert as a witness. (2) If a party serves a notice of intention under subrule (1), no objection may be made at trial to entering the expert's report as evidence unless, within 2 months after service of the notice under subrule (1), any other party serves a statement on the party serving the notice of intention (a) setting out all or parts of the report that that other party objects to being entered as evidence under this rule, and giving reasons for the objection, or (b) serving on the party a request that the expert attend the trial for cross-examination. (3) Agreeing to have the expert's report entered as evidence without calling the expert as a witness, either explicitly or by allowing subrule (2) to operate without objection, is not an admission of the truth or correctness of the expert's report.
